transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, it's... it's a few things, but honestly, what finally pushed me to make this appointment is just how much I'm struggling at work lately. I'm an auditor, and you know, the job requires a lot of follow-through. And I've been doing this for a long time, but recently, it's like... I keep starting these follow-up items. Like, after an audit is mostly wrapped up, or even after these mentorship events I help run for the junior staff, I'll sit down with every intention of finishing the paperwork or sending the final emails. I'll get all the files open on my computer, I'll even start typing up the review notes, and I tell myself, "Okay, I'm just going to knock this out right now." But then, somehow, I'll get sidetracked or I'll think I finished it, and then days later—literally days later—I'll get a ping from a partner or a client, and I find out that the final email, or the review note, or the compliance form never actually got done. It's just sitting there in my drafts, or I just completely abandoned it halfway through. And it's so embarrassing because I know I started it, I remember sitting there doing it, but I just... didn't finish. It's happening all the time now, and it's making me look so unprofessional.
Do you think you actually forget that you haven't finished these tasks, or do you remember that they're incomplete but have trouble getting back to them?

Well, it's... it's a bit of both, honestly, but a lot of times I genuinely just forget. I mean, completely forget. It's not like I'm sitting there thinking, "Oh, I really need to finish that email, I'll do it in five minutes," and then I just procrastinate. No, it's more like... it just leaves my brain entirely. And it's not just the big work things, either. It bleeds into everything. Like, I'll be talking to one of the junior staff members—because, like I said, I do a lot of mentoring, which I love, I really do, it's one of the best parts of the job—and they'll ask me a question that I need to look up. I'll say, "Give me ten minutes, let me check the prior year workpapers, and I'll call you right back." And I mean it! I absolutely mean to call them back. I'll even pull up the file. But then the phone rings, or I see an email from a partner, and... poof. The junior staff member is just gone from my mind until they message me three hours later asking if I found anything. 

And it happens with personal stuff, too, which is just so frustrating. Like, paying bills. I know I have a bill due, I'll even have the paper statement sitting right on my kitchen counter where I can see it, and I'll think, "I need to pay that before Friday so I don't get a late fee." But then Friday comes and goes, and I don't even realize I missed it until the next statement comes with the penalty attached. Or, back to the mentoring thing—I'll agree to host a lunch-and-learn or a roundtable for the new hires. I'll be in the meeting, I'll say, "Yes, absolutely, Thursday the 14th works perfectly for me," and then I just... don't put it on my calendar. I don't know why! I know I need to do it, but I get distracted by the next topic in the meeting, and then I completely forget about the event until someone sends a reminder the day before and I realize I double-booked myself. It's just this constant feeling of things slipping through the cracks, and I don't even realize they've slipped until they crash on the floor.
Do you find it hard to focus on tasks or pay attention to details?

Oh, absolutely. Yes. It's... it's actually one of the things that's causing me the most anxiety right now, to be perfectly honest with you. Because, you know, in auditing, detail is literally the job. It's supposed to be my strength. I've built my whole career on being the person who catches the things other people miss. But lately, it's like I can't even trust my own eyes anymore. 

Like, I'll be reviewing a report—a report I've done a hundred times, something I know backward and forward, where I absolutely know better than to rush. I know I need to take my time. But I'll be going through it, and I'll think I'm paying attention, I really do. And then it goes to the partner for final sign-off, and it comes back with all these red marks for the most ridiculous, careless mistakes. I'll miss a changed date from the prior year, so it still says 2022 instead of 2023. Or I'll transpose a number in a spreadsheet, which throws the whole variance analysis off. Or, and this is the one that just makes me want to crawl under my desk and hide... I'll leave a placeholder comment right in the middle of a final workpaper. Like, literally, it'll just say "insert explanation here" or "check with client on this," and I just completely sailed right past it when I was doing my review. 

And it's just... it's humiliating. It really is. Because the younger staff, the ones I'm supposed to be mentoring and setting an example for, they're looking at these files too. And here I am, the senior auditor, leaving placeholder text in a finalized document. It's not that I don't know how to do the work, or that I don't care—I care so much, maybe too much, which is why I'm sitting here talking to you—but it's like my brain just glazes over the details. I'll be looking right at the mistake, right at the transposed number, and my brain just registers it as correct. It's like I can't force myself to focus closely enough to actually see what's on the page anymore. It's exhausting, honestly, having to constantly double and triple-check myself and still finding out I missed something so obvious.
Do you have trouble organizing your time or tasks?

You know, actually... I don't think so. I mean, not really. It's funny you ask that, because I think people always assume that if you're dropping the ball on finishing things, or if you're making careless mistakes, your whole desk must be a disaster area or you just don't know what you're supposed to be doing. But honestly, my organization is probably the only thing keeping me afloat right now. I have this whole system I've used for years, and I'm very strict with myself about it. 

Every Monday morning, I get to the office—or I log on if I'm working from home—at 7:30 sharp. Before anyone else is even online, before the emails start pouring in from the partners, I sit down with my planner. And I don't just use Outlook, I actually use a physical paper planner because I feel like I need to physically write it down to make it real, you know? I color-code everything. Blue is for client meetings, red is for internal hard deadlines, green is for the mentorship stuff, which takes up a surprising amount of my week... I even block out specific chunks of time, down to the half-hour, just for reviewing the junior staff's workpapers so they aren't sitting around waiting on me. 

So, knowing what I need to do, or putting it in a logical order, or setting up the timeline... that part is actually fine. I can map out an entire six-week audit schedule for a team of five people, coordinate with the client's controller, and tell you exactly what phase of testing we should be in by next Tuesday. The structure is all there, and I know how to prioritize. It's just... well, like I was saying before, it's the actually executing it in the moment without getting derailed, or missing a detail when I'm in the thick of it. 

But the actual organizing of the time itself, or figuring out my tasks? No, I wouldn't say I struggle with that at all. I'm actually pretty meticulous about planning my week out. If anything, I probably spend a little too much time organizing my tasks because it feels productive, you know? Like, if I have a perfectly color-coded list, I feel like I'm in control, even if... well, even if I end up leaving a placeholder in the document anyway. But yeah, the organizing part I think I have a pretty good handle on.
Do you often find yourself forgetting things that happened recently?

No, actually... no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's really interesting that you ask that, because my husband sometimes gets frustrated and confused by this too. He'll say to me, "How can you remember exactly what the contractor said three weeks ago about the kitchen tile, but you can't remember to actually call him back?" And I try to explain to him—and I guess this is what I'm saying to you now—that my memory for things that have actually *happened* is completely fine. It's actually really sharp! 

Like, if I have a conversation with a client, or if I'm in a long meeting with the audit committee, I can usually recall exactly who said what. I can even remember the tone of voice the CFO used when he was trying to explain away a weird expense variance, you know? I don't forget events or conversations. Just the other day, that junior staff member I was telling you about, she was trying to recall how we handled a specific revenue recognition issue last year, and I remembered the exact client and the exact workaround we used without even having to look at my notes. So my brain definitely holds onto information and events that have already occurred. 

It's just... it's the future things, if that makes sense? The things I haven't done yet, the tasks that are pending or the emails I need to send. That's where the blank spot is. But if you're asking if I forget, like, what I had for breakfast, or if I had a conversation with someone this morning, or what happened in a meeting I just walked out of... no, never. My memory for actual events is rock solid. I can tell you everything that happened yesterday in excruciating detail. It's just the to-do list in my head that completely evaporates.
Do you often find yourself getting distracted by things around you?

Oh, constantly. It is... it's honestly ridiculous how easily I get pulled away. I mean, I try to set myself up for success, I really do, but it's like my brain is just constantly scanning for anything other than what I'm supposed to be doing. 

Like, if I'm trying to review an audit file—which, as I said, is already a minefield for me right now—I'll be right in the middle of tracing a complex transaction, and then... *ding*. A Slack ping comes through. And it doesn't even matter if it's important! It could literally be a junior staffer asking if there are leftover bagels in the breakroom, but my focus just snaps right to it. I can't ignore it. I have to look. And once I look, my train of thought on the audit is just completely derailed. 

And even if I mute my notifications, which I try to do when I really need to hunker down, it's the physical environment too. If someone is just talking outside my office... I mean, I can't just tune it out like a normal person. I'll hear two managers discussing a different engagement in the hallway, and suddenly I'm fully invested in their conversation, eavesdropping and analyzing what they're saying, and I've completely stopped working. 

But the worst part is, it doesn't even have to be something happening externally! It's my own head, too. I could be in a dead-silent room, staring at a spreadsheet, and out of nowhere, a thought about my marathon training will just pop into my brain. I'm running Chicago this fall, and suddenly I'll be sitting there wondering if I need to move my 18-miler to Sunday because of the rain forecast, or if I should switch up the brand of energy gels I'm using because the last ones made me kind of nauseous. And before I know it, I'm deep down an internet rabbit hole about running nutrition, and twenty minutes have gone by, and that audit file is just sitting there untouched on my second monitor. 

It's like... a Slack ping, the hallway noise, my own random thoughts about running... literally anything can pull me completely off track. It takes so much energy just to constantly drag myself back to the page.
Do you often feel restless or fidgety when you're trying to sit still?

Oh, absolutely. It is... well, it's actually really uncomfortable for me to just sit there and do nothing with my body. Especially during those long audit committee meetings, or when we have our all-hands staff meetings on Friday afternoons. I mean, they book these things for two, sometimes three hours, and they expect everyone to just sit perfectly still in these terrible conference room chairs that are supposed to be ergonomic but really aren't, and I just... I just can't do it. I am always moving something. 

When I'm sitting in meetings, I'm usually tapping my foot under the table, or I find myself clicking my pen over and over. I try to catch myself because I know the clicking can drive people crazy, but if I force myself to stop doing that, I just end up shifting in the chair constantly instead. Crossing my legs, uncrossing them, leaning forward, leaning back, adjusting my posture. It's actually gotten to the point where one of my colleagues—she's a senior manager I work really closely with on a lot of our manufacturing clients—she actually joked the other day that she doesn't even need to look over to know I'm sitting next to her, because she can literally hear my leg going under the table. 

Which is, you know, a little embarrassing when you really think about it. I mean, I'm a professional, I should be able to sit through a PowerPoint presentation about Q3 deliverables without bouncing around, right? But it's like this physical tension just builds up in my legs, and if I don't move, I feel like I'm going to crawl out of my skin. It takes so much conscious effort for me to freeze my body, and if I'm putting all my energy into just sitting still, then I'm definitely not absorbing whatever the CFO is saying anyway. So yeah, I am definitely restless, I just can't seem to turn that physical motor off.
Do you often act on impulse without fully thinking things through?

No, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive. I mean, I really don't think so. It's funny you ask that, because I know people sometimes associate being, you know, easily distracted or a little fidgety with being reckless, but that's really not me at all. In fact, in my line of work—being an auditor—you really can't afford to just act without thinking. Everything I do has to be documented, reviewed, cross-referenced... I mean, the whole nature of the job is about being methodical and analyzing the risks before you make a move. 

If anything, I think I overthink things, especially when it comes to making decisions. Like, if I'm looking at a client's internal controls, I'm not just going to jump to a conclusion and write up a deficiency without really digging into the underlying data and thinking through all the possible implications. I'll sit there and agonize over the wording of a management letter comment for an hour just to make sure it's exactly right. 

And even outside of work, like with my marathon training... I don't just go out and run on impulse. I have a very specific, structured 16-week training block. I plan out my mileage, my pace targets, my recovery days. I research everything. I mentioned the energy gels earlier—I spent probably two hours reading reviews and looking at the carbohydrate ratios before I bought a new box. So I'm definitely not the type of person to just do something on a whim or make a snap decision without considering the consequences. I mean, sure, I might get distracted by an article about running shoes when I should be working, but I'm not going to just impulsively buy a $250 pair of carbon-plated racers without thinking it through. I'm actually pretty cautious, all things considered. So, no, I don't think I act on impulse at all.
Do you often feel anxious or overwhelmed, even when you're not dealing with a specific stressful situation?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I definitely get stressed out, but it's always tied to something specific, you know? Like, right now, we're in the middle of busy season, and the sheer volume of work is just crushing. I've got three different clients going through their quarterly reviews, and the deadlines are just stacked right on top of each other. So, yes, I feel overwhelmed, but who wouldn't? It's a completely normal reaction to the workload. 

And even outside of busy season, if I'm feeling anxious, it's usually because I'm worried about something concrete. Like last month, I was stressing over this big presentation I had to give to a new client's board of directors. I spent weeks preparing for it, making sure every slide was perfect, anticipating every possible question they could ask. I was definitely anxious leading up to it, but once the presentation was over, the anxiety was gone. It's not like this free-floating feeling of dread that just hangs over me for no reason. 

I mean, I've had colleagues who talk about waking up with their heart pounding, just feeling this overwhelming sense of panic, even when everything in their life is going fine. And I really feel for them, I do, because that sounds awful. But I just don't relate to that at all. My stress is very situational. If I have a 60-hour work week ahead of me, or if my marathon training plan calls for a 20-miler and it's pouring rain, yeah, I'm going to feel a little overwhelmed. But if I'm just sitting on the couch on a Sunday afternoon with nothing on my to-do list? No, I'm perfectly fine. I don't just feel anxious out of nowhere.
Do you have trouble managing your emotions when you're under pressure or stressed?

No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, I think I'm actually pretty good at keeping my emotions in check, even when things get really, really intense. I know some people completely lose it when the pressure is on—they snap at their coworkers, or they start crying in the bathroom, or they just shut down completely. But I don't really do any of that. 

Like, just last week, we had this massive crisis with a client. It's a mid-sized manufacturing firm I've been auditing for about four years now, and their controller called me at 4:30 on a Thursday, right before a major filing deadline, to tell me they had completely restated their inventory valuation for the last two quarters. Which, if you know anything about auditing, is basically a nightmare scenario at the eleventh hour. It changes everything—the cost of goods sold, the margins, the tax implications, it is just a huge cascading mess. And I could hear the absolute panic in his voice, he was practically hyperventilating over the phone because he knew how bad it was. 

But I didn't freak out. I didn't yell at him, even though I was incredibly frustrated internally, and I didn't break down. I just took a breath, pulled up the new spreadsheets he sent over, and started mapping out exactly what we needed to do to trace the new numbers. My junior staff were all looking at me like the sky was falling, and I just calmly delegated the tasks. I told one person to take the Q2 adjustments, I had another pull the new warehouse receipts, and we just got to work. I think because I'm so focused on the methodical, analytical part of the job, the emotional part just doesn't really take over. I just immediately go into problem-solving mode. 

And it's the exact same way with my running. If I'm at mile 18 of a marathon and my calves start cramping up and I realize I'm slipping behind my pace group, I don't start crying or get angry at myself. I just assess the situation. I ask myself if I need more sodium, or if I need to adjust my stride, or if I just need to mentally push through the wall. So, no, I don't really have emotional outbursts or lose control when I'm stressed out. I just put my head down and deal with the logistics of whatever the problem is. If anything, I think people rely on me to be the calm one when the pressure is on, because I just don't let my emotions get the better of me in those situations.
Do you often struggle to motivate yourself to start tasks or activities?

No, I wouldn't say I struggle with motivation at all. Honestly, I'm kind of the exact opposite. I'm very much a self-starter. I mean, if you look at my daily routine, there's really no room for sitting around and waiting for motivation to strike, you know? Like, I'm up at 5:00 AM every single morning. I don't even hit snooze. I just roll out of bed, put on my running gear—which I always lay out the night before, right down to the socks and my heart rate monitor, because it just removes any friction from the morning—and I'm out the door by 5:15. I don't sit on the edge of the bed debating whether or not I feel like running. I just get up and do it. 

And it's the exact same way with my job. When I sit down at my desk at 8:00 AM—well, usually it's more like 7:30 or 7:45, because I really like to get a head start on clearing out my inbox before the partners start messaging me with requests—I don't just stare at the screen. I have my checklist, I open up the audit software, pull up the prior year workpapers, and I just dive right in. I mean, sure, there are definitely tasks I don't particularly enjoy doing. Like, nobody likes doing substantive testing on operating expenses. It is incredibly tedious, just pulling hundreds of invoices and checking authorization signatures for hours on end. It's mind-numbing. But I don't sit around struggling to start it. I know it has to be done for the file, so I just open the spreadsheet and start ticking and tying the numbers. 

I think a lot of that just comes down to discipline. I've always been that way, even back when I was getting my bachelor's degree. You don't survive intermediate accounting if you can't motivate yourself to open the textbook and just do the practice problems, you know? So when I hear people talk about procrastination, or needing to, like, find their motivation before they can tackle a project, I just... I don't really relate to that. If something is on my schedule, whether it's drafting a memo for a client, doing a 10-mile tempo run, or even just doing the grocery shopping on a Sunday morning, I just execute it. I don't have that barrier to getting started. So, no, getting motivated to start things really isn't an issue for me.
Do you often experience feelings of sadness or hopelessness?

No, I really don't. I mean, I definitely don't feel hopeless. Sadness... well, sure, if something genuinely sad happens, but as a general, everyday feeling? No, not at all. I think I'm just too practical for that. Or honestly, probably just too busy! When you're auditing financial statements for 60 hours a week and then trying to squeeze in a 40-mile running week on top of that, there really isn't a lot of time to sit around feeling hopeless. 

I think hopelessness usually comes when people feel like they don't have control over their lives, you know? Like they're just drifting. But I'm the exact opposite of drifting. Every hour of my day is pretty much accounted for. I even color-code my Outlook calendar—blue for client meetings, green for internal reviews, orange for my personal training blocks. So I always know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing. I look at my life, and I feel pretty good about where I am at 47. I've built up a solid reputation with the partners at my firm, they know they can hand me a messy file and I'll just get it done. 

So when I look at the big picture, I don't feel sad. I mean, sure, I get frustrated if a client doesn't upload their trial balance to the secure portal when they promised they would, or if I have a bad run where my splits are, like, 30 seconds slower than my target pace. But that's frustration, not sadness. It's just a problem to solve. I don't spiral into thinking, 'oh, what's the point of it all.' I just think, 'Okay, I need to send a firm follow-up email to the controller,' or 'I need to spend an extra twenty minutes foam rolling my hamstrings tonight.' It's all very action-oriented. I just don't really have the bandwidth to sit and dwell on sad thoughts, if that makes sense? I'm just very focused on moving forward, ticking things off the list, and getting to the next deadline.
Do you find it hard to maintain your focus on a single task for an extended period of time?

You know, this is actually... yes. This is something that really bothers me, especially because, like I said, I'm so disciplined in every other area of my life. But keeping my focus locked in for a long stretch? That is a real struggle, and it's been getting on my nerves lately. 

For example, our firm has been rolling out all these mandatory continuing education sessions on this new AI-assisted auditing tool. It's supposed to automate a lot of our sample selections and initial risk assessments, which sounds great in theory, but the training sessions are these massive, dense, three-hour virtual seminars. And I'll log in, I've got my notepad right next to my keyboard, my coffee is fresh, and I start out fully engaged. I'm taking meticulous notes, I'm tracking exactly what the presenter is saying about the data extraction protocols, I'm totally dialed in. 

But then... I don't even know how it happens, really, but after a while, my mind just completely slips off. It's not like I'm getting up and walking away or scrolling through my phone under the desk. I am physically sitting right there, staring directly at the monitor. But suddenly I'll kind of snap back to reality, and I realize the presenter is on a completely different slide, talking about a totally different module, and I have absolutely no idea what was said for the last five or ten minutes. I've completely missed it, even though I was looking right at the screen the entire time. 

And it's not just the trainings, the exact same thing happens during long client meetings. We do these extensive quarterly planning meetings with the CFOs and controllers, and they can easily drag on for two, sometimes two and a half hours. I'll be right there on the Teams call, or sitting at the conference table, nodding along, maintaining perfect eye contact with whoever is speaking. But internally, my brain has just... gone somewhere else. I'll be mentally calculating my marathon pacing for the weekend, or thinking about how I need to reformat a specific Excel workbook, or sometimes just thinking about absolutely nothing at all. And then the client will pause, or I'll realize they've moved from discussing accounts receivable over to payroll liabilities, and I just have this spike of panic because I missed the entire transition. It's incredibly frustrating because I really am trying to pay attention. I know the information is critical for the audit file, but it's like my brain just quietly unplugs itself from the audio while my eyes are still open and pretending to watch.
Do you ever find yourself so intensely focused on a task that you lose track of everything else around you?

No, I don't think I ever do that. Actually, I know I don't. I'm... I'm way too aware of the clock for that to ever happen. You have to understand, in my line of work, time is literally everything. We bill our clients in six-minute increments, so my entire professional life for the last twenty-something years has been governed by the timer on my screen. I could be deep into the most complicated, multi-tab Excel workbook you've ever seen—like, doing a massive reconciliation of intercompany accounts where the client has completely botched the foreign currency conversions, which happens way more often than you'd think—and I still know exactly what time it is. I never just 'lose myself' in the spreadsheet. 

And it's the same with my physical surroundings. I'm always very tuned in to what's going on around me. If I'm working at the office, I know exactly who is walking past my desk, I hear the printer down the hall spinning up, I notice when the senior partner's door opens. I never get so zoned in that the world just fades away. Honestly, sometimes when I hear people talk about that—like artists or writers who say they just started working, looked up, and suddenly five hours had passed without them even noticing—I almost envy them a little bit? Because my brain just does not work that way. I am constantly checking the time, constantly looking at my color-coded Outlook schedule to see what the next block is, constantly aware of my environment. 

Even when I'm running, you know, doing a long 15-miler on a Sunday morning, I'm checking my Garmin watch every single half mile to check my pace and make sure I'm staying in the right heart rate zone. I don't just zone out and forget where I am or how long I've been out there. I'm always completely anchored to the reality of the moment and the schedule. I always know exactly how much time has passed. So, no, getting so absorbed in something that I lose track of time or what's going on around me... that's just not something I experience. At all.
Do you find it hard to maintain your attention on a single task for a long time?

Wait, didn't we just touch on this a second ago? With the... the virtual trainings and the client meetings? But, yes, absolutely, it is a huge issue for me. It's exactly like I was saying just a minute ago. 

I can start out totally, one hundred percent engaged. Take those long quarterly client meetings or that massive AI-tool training our firm is making us do. I'll sit down, I’ve got my notepad out, my pen is ready, I’m making perfect eye contact with the speaker or the monitor, and I am completely dialed in to the agenda. I’m ready to tackle it, taking detailed notes on the risk assessments or whatever it is. 

But then, after a while... it’s like a switch just flips without me even noticing. My mind just completely slips off. I’ll be staring right at the screen, physically present, looking like the model employee, but internally, I am miles away. I’ll start thinking about my marathon training schedule, or wondering if I sent that one specific email to the junior auditor about the inventory count, or just... thinking about nothing at all, just floating. And then I’ll suddenly snap back to reality because the presenter changes their tone or asks a question, and I realize I’ve completely missed the last five or ten minutes of the presentation. 

And the most frustrating part of the whole thing is that I’m still looking exactly where I’m supposed to be looking! It’s not like I’m playing on my phone under the desk or looking out the window. My eyes are locked right on the screen, but my brain has just quietly walked out the back door. It drives me absolutely crazy because, like I said, I really *want* to pay attention, I know I *need* to know this stuff for the audit files, but I just cannot hold that focus for the whole stretch, no matter how hard I try to force it.
Do you find it hard to keep your attention on a task for as long as you need to?

I'm sorry, but are we... didn't I just answer this? I feel like we're stuck on a loop here, doctor. Is there a specific detail you're looking for that I'm leaving out? Because, yes. Yes, I do. It is exactly what I was just explaining to you about those long client meetings and the mandatory AI-tool trainings. 

I mean, I can keep repeating it if you need me to, but the pattern is always exactly the same. I know the stakes, I know I *need* to keep my attention on the task for the full duration—whether it's a two-hour quarterly review or a massive three-hour seminar on automated sample selections. And I always start out so strong. I am fully engaged. I sit down at my desk, I have my legal pad perfectly aligned, my pens are out, and I am ready to absorb every single detail because, as an auditor, I can't afford to just guess what the new risk assessment protocols are. 

But then, despite all my best intentions, my mind just slips off. It just drifts completely away, and I don't even feel it happening. It’s not a conscious choice. I'll be sitting there, staring directly at my monitor, looking right at the CFO or the trainer, maintaining what looks like absolute, perfect professional focus. But internally? I'm not absorbing a single word. I'm just gone. And then the presenter will change their tone of voice, or ask if there are any questions, and I'll just snap back to reality with this horrible, sinking feeling in my stomach because I realize I've missed the last five or ten minutes entirely. Even though I was looking right at the screen the whole time! 

So, yes, keeping my attention locked in for as long as I actually *need* to is exactly the problem. I really don't know how else to explain it, it's just... it's incredibly exhausting trying to force my brain to stay on track when it clearly just wants to unplug.
Do you think your difficulties with focus and completing tasks are affecting your daily life and relationships?

Yes. I mean, honestly, that's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you today. It is bleeding into literally every aspect of my life, and it's getting to the point where I just can't hide it anymore. 

At work... well, I’m supposed to be on track for a pretty major promotion this year. But lately, my mistakes—just these stupid, careless little things—and my unfinished follow-ups have gotten so out of hand that it actually affected a major client review last month. I was supposed to tie out the remaining workpapers and follow up with the client's controller on some missing documentation for their inventory valuation. And I just... I don't even know what happened. I kept putting it off, or I’d start the email and get distracted, and I just never finished it. The deadline hit, the file was incomplete, and the senior partner had to step in and smooth things over with the client. It was incredibly humiliating. Now I am constantly, constantly worrying that the partners are talking about me behind closed doors, questioning whether I can actually handle this promotion. Because if I can't even manage my own open-items list, how on earth am I going to manage a whole department? 

And then at home, it’s... it's honestly just as bad, if not worse, because it's so embarrassing. I’m a CPA, right? My entire professional career is built on financial accuracy and deadlines. But my husband has had to completely take over paying our household bills. I think a lot of that just comes down to discipline. I've always been that way, even back when I was getting my bachelor's degree. So when I hear people talk about procrastination, or needing to, like, find their motivation before they can tackle a project, I just... I don't really relate to that. I don't have that barrier to getting started. So, no, getting motivated to start things really isn't an issue for me.
